1868395.fragment:
Liliata rutilantium.
 Turma circumdet.
 Iubilantium te virginum

range.content:
Liliata rutilantium.
 Turma circumdet.
 Iubilantium te virginum

1868395.twitter_share_message: “Liliata rutilantium te confessorum turma circumdet: iubilantium te virginum chorus excipiat, tra…” —@Genius

children: Liliata rutilantium te confessorum turma circumdet: iubilantium te virginum chorus excipiat,
translates as:
May the troop of confessors, glowing like lilies, surround you. May the choir of virgins, jubilant, take you in.
The source of these words is in the Prayers for the Dying in the Catholic Layman’s Missal.

The Missal contains instructions on the acceptable use of the prayer: “In the absence of a priest, these prayers for commending a dying person to God, may be read by any responsible person, man or woman.” The prayer was chanted, then, by one or more of the family members who “prayed on their knees” while gathered around the bedside of Stephen’s dying mother, as Stephen recalls in Telemachus the first time he thinks of the Latin lines. Stephen continues to recall snatches of the two sentences during the rest of his day: once more in Telemachus, once in Aeolus, once in Circe, and once in Ithaca.
Joyce Project

1868422.fragment: The Ship, Buck Mulligan cried. Half twelve.

range.content: The Ship, Buck Mulligan cried. Half twelve.

1868422.twitter_share_message: “Telemachus ships out of Ithaca at the end of Book 2 of The Odyssey, to inquire about his father …” —@Genius

children: Telemachus ships out of Ithaca at the end of Book 2 of The Odyssey, to inquire about his father on the mainland. On his return at the end of Book 4, Antinous and nineteen other suitors lie in ambush for him behind an island that he must pass. Athena helps him to escape the deadly trap.

Similarly, Stephen will evade his antagonist. Instead of meeting Mulligan at “The Ship,” the downtown tavern that has figured in their conversation earlier in their chapter, at the appointed time of “Half twelve” (i.e., 12:30), he sends him a taunting telegram from only a short distance away. We learn of this development in Scylla and Charybdis, when Mulligan finds Stephen in the library (Stephen thinks, “Hast thou found me, O mine enemy?”). Mulligan reads the telegram with delight, and asks, “Where did you launch it from?”
Joyce Project

range.content: Usurper.

1868441.twitter_share_message:
“From the Joyce Project:


Telemachus begins with “Stately, plump Buck Mulligan” seen through thi…” —@Genius

children: From the
Joyce Project:

Telemachus begins with “Stately, plump Buck Mulligan” seen through third-person narration that approaches his own subjective position, though the narrative voice is quickly pulled into the orbit of the lean and hungry Stephen. The episode ends with the same person seen entirely through Stephen’s eyes, as a “Usurper” similar to Claudius and Antinous.

Mulligan cooperates in this coercive casting by taking the key to the tower from Stephen, which Stephen regards as usurpation because he “paid the rent.“ In a less literal sense, Stephen may feel usurped because Mulligan would insinuate himself into a position of authority in his life—a life whose credo is evading subjection. In Circe, as Stephen approaches the climax of desperation signaled by his mother’s ghoulish appearance from the dead, he cries out against his "foes,” one in particular: “Break my spirit, will he?” The “he” remains unspecified, but no one is more likely than Buck.
PROPOSED SUGGESTION: usurper: someone who wrongfully takes someone’s place

Throughout this chapter, the sea, ‘our mother’ makes Stephen slip into thoughts of his mother. But when he peers into the sea he is frustrated by his consciousness noticing the seal, which interrupts (replaces) his poetic stream of thought.

children: A list of early heretics.

Photius, while not a heretic in the usual sense, was deposed by the Fourth [Roman Catholic] Council of Constantinople (869-870) from his position as Patriarch of Constantinople, the head of the Eastern (today, Eastern Orthodox) Church. This was in part because he was a layman when he was appointed to the Patriarchate. This was the first council that was not recognized by both East and West, and an early indicator of the approaching 1054 schism.

Arius (256-336) believed that Jesus Christ was not of the same essence of God, and was only the first creation of the Father. His promulgation of this teaching was the impetus for the calling of the Council of Nicaea in 325, the very first ecumenical council.

Valentine, more commonly called Valentinus, lived from c.100-c.160, and was a Christian gnostic theologian who believed that the material world was evil, and to some extent denied the incarnation of Christ.
Sabellius (3rd century) was a Christian priest who taught that God was not three persons, but three manifestations of the same person.
Arius, Valentinus, and Sabellius all held anti-Trinitarian views that were rejected and condemned by orthodox Christianity.
